proof:
# A Grünbaum-level cap circuit restores global BM rigidity

This is a scoped rigidity theorem. It explains a sufficient additional
condition under which the captured-side equality cover really does force
whole-body equality. Its ordinary geometric input is the classical
Grünbaum theorem and its single-cap pyramid equality case, precisely as
recorded and used in the independently audited note
`candidate e2c55c91458e1e8c`, Section 1.
No mixed-integer inequality or extremizer classification is invoked.

## 1. Exact theorem

Let d>=2. Let A,B,K be full-dimensional compact convex bodies in R^d,
with (A+B)/2 subset K. Let y belong to int(K). Let

    H_i={x:u_i.(x-y)>=0}, i=1,...,m,

where the nonzero normals form a minimal positive circuit: there are
alpha_i>0 with sum alpha_i u_i=0, and no proper subfamily has such a
positive dependence. Suppose:

1. Every cut A intersect H_i and B intersect H_i is proper.
2. For each i the captured-side BM comparison is exactly tight:

       |K intersect H_i|^(1/d)
          =(|A intersect H_i|^(1/d)+|B intersect H_i|^(1/d))/2.

3. Every source cap has the continuous extremal fraction:

       |K intersect H_i|=Gamma_d |K|,
       Gamma_d=(d/(d+1))^d.

Here a proper cut means that its boundary hyperplane meets the interior
of the body. Equivalently, both its captured side and its strict
complement have positive full-dimensional volume.

Then m=d+1, K is a d-simplex, y is its centroid, and A,B are positive
homothetic simplices. Moreover K=(A+B)/2 and whole-body BM is an
equality. No assumption that y was an ordinary deepest point or the
centroid is needed.

## 2. The source is the actual Minkowski midpoint

Put D=(A+B)/2. The positive circuit makes the H_i cover R^d: if all
u_i.(x-y) were negative, their positively weighted sum would be negative.
For each i the endpoint caps have positive volume. Convexity gives

    (A intersect H_i+B intersect H_i)/2
        subset D intersect H_i subset K intersect H_i.

Brunn--Minkowski and hypothesis 2 show that the leftmost and rightmost
sets have the same positive volume. A strict inclusion between compact
full-dimensional convex bodies has strictly different volume. One proof
is to strictly separate a point of the larger body from the smaller and
take a small simplex with that point and an interior ball of the larger
body; a positive-volume part lies beyond the smaller support plane.
Consequently these cap sets are equal, in particular

    K intersect H_i subset D.

Taking their union and using the cover gives K subset D. Thus K=D.

## 3. The ordinary centroid lies on every cut plane

Let g be the ordinary centroid of K. If u_i.(g-y)>0 for any i, the
through-g parallel cap is a strict smaller subset of K intersect H_i.
The difference contains an open slab inside K because g is interior,
so its volume is positive. Ordinary Grünbaum would then give

    |K intersect H_i|
       >|K intersect {u_i.(x-g)>=0}|
       >=Gamma_d |K|,

contrary to hypothesis 3. Hence u_i.(g-y)<=0 for every i. Their
positive balance forces each of these numbers to be zero. Therefore
all the H_i are centroid cuts and are equality caps in ordinary
Grünbaum.

The standard single-cap equality characterization now supplies, for
each i, a pyramid representation

    K=conv(v_i,F_i),

where F_i is in a hyperplane parallel to the cut and v_i is its apex
on the captured side. Let lambda_i be the affine height, zero on F_i
and one at v_i. Then lambda_i>=0 on K, its gradient is a positive
multiple of u_i, and its volume mean is 1/(d+1). The last assertion
also follows directly by integrating pyramid sections, whose areas
at height t are proportional to (1-t)^(d-1).

## 4. Balanced equality pyramids force a simplex and identify y

Every extreme point of a pyramid other than its apex lies in its base:
a point of intermediate height lies strictly between its apex and a
point of the base. Distinct circuit directions have distinct apices.
Indeed, for a fixed apex the other extreme points span the unique
full-dimensional base hyperplane, determining its oriented normal.
Minimality of the positive circuit excludes repeated positive directions.
Thus

    lambda_i(v_j)=1 if i=j, and zero otherwise.

Rescale the positive balancing coefficients to beta_i>0 with
sum beta_i grad(lambda_i)=0. The affine function sum beta_i lambda_i
is constant. Evaluating at v_j shows that this constant is every beta_j,
and is positive. Therefore

    sum_i lambda_i=1.

Integrating over K gives m/(d+1)=1, so m=d+1. Applying the lambda_i
to an affine dependence of the v_j shows that the vertices are affinely
independent. Their convex hull is contained in K, and the nonnegative
affine barycentric coordinates lambda_i place K inside that same hull.
Hence K is their simplex.

The gradients of the d+1 simplex barycentric functions span R^d, so
the u_i also span R^d. Section 3 therefore yields g-y=0. Thus y is
the actual centroid, rather than a selected point merely assumed to
have that property.

This also supplies a direct proof of the equality-rigidity step that
one could alternatively obtain from the archived ordinary maximal-depth
theorem. In that alternative proof, the cap cover bounds the ordinary
depth of every point by Gamma_d, and Grünbaum supplies the reverse
bound at the centroid.

## 5. Elementary indecomposability of a full-dimensional simplex

For completeness, let K=conv{v_0,...,v_d} be a full-dimensional simplex
and suppose A+B=2K with A,B full dimensional. Choose decompositions

    2v_i=a_i+b_i, a_i in A, b_i in B.

If a vector w uniquely exposes v_i in K, the support identity
h_A(w)+h_B(w)=2h_K(w) forces a_i,b_i to maximize their respective
supports. Their exposed faces must be singletons, since their Minkowski
sum is the singleton {2v_i}. This conclusion holds for every w in
the open normal cone of v_i with the same fixed decomposition.

The union of these open vertex normal cones is dense among all
directions. On it, h_A(w)=max_i w.a_i. By continuity the same equality
holds for every w, proving A=conv{a_i}. Similarly B=conv{b_i}. Full
dimension makes each list of d+1 vertices affinely independent.

For each i!=j, a supporting vector exposing the simplex edge [v_i,v_j]
gives

    F_A(w)+F_B(w)=2[v_i,v_j].

The first face contains a_i,a_j and the second b_i,b_j. Therefore
a_j-a_i and b_j-b_i are parallel to v_j-v_i. Their scalar ratios are
positive: a vector uniquely exposing v_i also uniquely exposes a_i,
and its scalar products with a_i-a_j and v_i-v_j are both positive.

Write a_i-a_0=t_i(v_i-v_0), with t_i>0, for i=1,...,d. The parallel
relation for an edge [v_i,v_j], and independence of v_i-v_0 and
v_j-v_0, force t_i=t_j. Hence there are v in R^d and lambda>0 such
that

    A=v+lambda K.

The vertex decompositions give B=-v+(2-lambda)K. Full dimension and
the same positive orientation give 2-lambda>0. Consequently both
summands are positively homothetic simplices, and

    (|A|^(1/d)+|B|^(1/d))/2
       =[lambda+(2-lambda)]|K|^(1/d)/2
       =|K|^(1/d).

This completes the theorem and its noncircular dependency chain.

## 6. Precise scope

The Gamma_d source-cap condition is a substantive ordinary extremal
condition. It is not supplied by captured-side BM equality alone: the
explicit proper positive-circuit quadrilaterals in
`candidate 60dfb1dd651b7ddd`
violate the global conclusion when this condition is removed. Nor does
the theorem show that any mixed-integer minimizing configuration has
these source cap fractions. That remains a separate global question.
